newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean president's son probed over payoff rumours.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean president's son probed over payoff rumours.

text.p: Police on Friday raided the offices of a South Korean businessman in a probe into rumours that President Kim Young-sam's son accepted a 200 billion won ($226 million) kickback, prosecution officials said.
State prosecutors were looking into rumours that Kim Hyun-chul took the money from the businessman acting as an agent for failed Hanbo Steel Co, they said.
"The purpose is to confirm rumours that Kim Hyun-chul accepted 200 billion won ($226 million)," one official told Reuters.

Hanbo Steel collapsed in January under debts of $5.8 billion in the country's biggest corporate failure. Ten people, including a former cabinet minister, are on trial for bribery over improper loans to the steelmaker.
Parliament on Friday kicked off an investigation into funding for Hanbo and will call Kim Hyun-chul to testify.

The ruling New Korea Party agreed to the parliamentary inquiry after opposition parties attacked an earlier probe by prosecutors as a whitewash that failed to bring to justice leading players in the scandal.
The Justice Ministry announced on Friday that the top prosecution investigator had been replaced.
Opposition parties have alleged that the president's second son peddled influence to keep loans to Hanbo rolling in.

Kim Hyun-chul issued an apology on Monday for causing trouble and anxiety and said he was ready to accept punishment if he had done wrong. His father said on television last month he felt shamed his son had been linked to the Hanbo scandal.
The younger Kim has no official posts but is dubbed by newspapers the "crown prince" and played a leading role in his father's election in 1992.
State radio and other national broadcasters said the businessman, Park Tae-joong, was a close associate of Kim Hyun-chul and managed his money.
Allegations that the president's son accepted money in connection with Hanbo first surfaced in parliament last month.

Opposition legislator Lim Chae-jung said there were strong suspicions that the president's son took more than 200 billion won as a rebate on the purchase of German-made equipment for a new mill being built by Hanbo Steel.

On Friday opposition parties demanded the parliamentary inquiry cover the collapse of a second steelmaker, Sammi Steel Co. They cited suspicions of influence peddling also involving the president's son.
Sammi Steel, the country's largest specialty steelmaker, and its trading affiliate Sammi Corp were declared insolvent on Thursday.
"We believe Sammi's default is another example of a sleazy politics-business alliance," said spokeswoman Park Sun-suck of the main opposition National Congress for New Politics.
The prosecution probe into Hanbo led by Choi Byung-koog exonerated Kim Hyun-chul.
"Some misunderstandings have occurred during the Hanbo investigation," a Justice Ministry statement said, explaining the decision to remove Choi.
"The replacement was made to ensure a transparent and fair investigation to reveal the truth."

Former cabinet minister Kim Woo-suk, close aides to President Kim Young-sam, Hanbo founder Chung Tae-soo and his chief accountant as well as three top bankers are standing trial in connection with the Hanbo scandal.
